theme: Blessed is the one who considers the poor
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 41. It closes the first book of the Psalter. Notice verse 9, which Jesus applies to Judas in John 13, and the blessing for those who care for the poor at the beginning.
settingTheScene: Psalm 41 is a psalm of David written in illness, when enemies gloated and a close friend turned against him. It begins with a beatitude for the one who considers the poor, and it ends with a doxology that closes the first of the five books of the Psalms. It comes in the plan at the point in Luke where the shadow of betrayal falls.
observation: “Blessed is the one who considers the poor! In the day of trouble the LORD delivers him” (v. 1).
“The LORD sustains him on his sickbed; in his illness you restore him to full health” (v. 3).
“As for me, I said, O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against you!” (v. 4).
“My enemies say of me in malice: When will he die, and his name perish?” (v. 5).
“Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me” (v. 9).
“By this I know that you delight in me: my enemy will not shout in triumph over me” (v. 11).
“But you have upheld me because of my integrity, and set me in your presence forever” (v. 12).
“Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! Amen and Amen” (v. 13).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a blessing on those who consider the poor. This means paying attention, thinking about, and caring for the weak. The reward is that the LORD delivers them in the day of trouble, protects them, keeps them alive, and sustains them on a sickbed.

Then David turns to his own distress. He is sick, and he prays, “O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against you!” He does not claim innocence. He asks for mercy, trusting that God’s grace is greater than his guilt.

His enemies wait for him to die. Visitors come with empty words, and then go out to spread slander. “They imagine the worst for me.” Then comes the sharpest pain: “Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me.” Betrayal by someone who shared your table is a particular kind of grief.

Jesus quotes this verse at the Last Supper (John 13:18) about Judas. David’s betrayal by his friend, probably Ahithophel, is a pattern of the greater betrayal of the Son of David. In Luke 22, Jesus eats the Passover with his betrayer at the table.

David asks to be raised up, so that he may repay them. But he trusts that God delights in him because the enemy has not triumphed. “You have upheld me because of my integrity, and set me in your presence forever.” David’s integrity is not sinlessness but the sincerity of one who has confessed and been forgiven. The end of the psalm is the doxology that closes Book I: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! Amen and Amen.”

For Christians, the one who truly considered the poor, who bore betrayal, and who was upheld and raised up forever, is Jesus.
connection: John 13:18 quotes verse 9. 2 Samuel 15 to 17 tells of Ahithophel’s betrayal of David. Matthew 26:14-16 and Luke 22:3-6 describe Judas’s betrayal. Proverbs 14:21 and 19:17 speak of kindness to the poor. Psalm 72:12-14 says the king delivers the needy. 2 Corinthians 8:9 says Christ became poor for our sake. Matthew 25:31-46 describes the judgment in terms of care for the least.
application:
Consider the poor this week: give, visit, or serve someone in need.

If you have been betrayed, bring it to the LORD in prayer. Forgive as he leads you.

Pray David’s prayer in verse 4 honestly, naming your sins and asking for grace.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to be gracious and heal you, and tell him your sin.
Ask him to teach you to consider the poor.
Thank Jesus, who knows the pain of betrayal.
